The Muirs were Scots in Philadelphia. William David Muir was born there in 1837 “of Scotch parents”,
and at fifteen went up to Hawley, in the hills of north-eastern Pennsylvania, to learn machining from his uncle,
William L. Stewart. It was coal and railroad country.
In the 1820s the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company had built a gravity railroad over the Moosic Mountains:
stationary steam engines hauled cars of anthracite from the mines at Carbondale up a chain of inclined planes,
and the cars ran down the far side by their own weight to Honesdale, where canal boats carried the coal 108 miles
to the Hudson and on to New York. Charlotte Stephens’s family had come over from Orange County,
New York, to the same township, Palmyra, by 1850, when her father was a butcher at Hawley;
she and William married in 1861. He helped raise Hawley’s company of the 141st Pennsylvania in 1862.
He was wounded at Gettysburg with the 141st Pennsylvania in 1863 and rose to division superintendent of the Gravity
Railroad, and they lived on Gravity Heights at Honesdale.
Charlotte’s people, the Stephenses, had come to Nicholson, west of the mountains,
in 1784, the first settlers there by the family’s account, and through them DeWitt’s mother’s line goes back to the
Mayflower. Their son William, a machinist like his father, married Anna Yeager,
whose German parents had landed in 1867 and lived at Honesdale until 1871, when they moved on to the coal city of
Wilkes-Barre. William took his own family to Atlantic City and then to Wilkes-Barre,
